This article consists of some loosely related remarks about the geometry of G_2-structures on 7-manifolds and is partly based on old unpublished joint work with two other people: F. Reese Harvey and Steven Altschuler. Much of this work has since been subsumed in the work of Hitchin \cite{MR02m:53070} and Joyce \cite{MR01k:53093}. I am making it available now mainly because of interest expressed by others in seeing these results written up since they do not seem to have all made it into the literature. A formula is derived for the scalar curvature and Ricci curvature of a G_2-structure in terms of its torsion. When the fundamental 3-form of the G_2-structure is closed, this formula implies, in particular, that the scalar curvature of the underlying metric is nonpositive and vanishes if and only if the structure is torsion-free. This version contains some new results on the pinching of Ricci curvature for metrics associated to closed G_2-structures. Some formulae are derived for closed solutions of the Laplacian flow that specify how various related quantities, such as the torsion and the metric, evolve with the flow. These may be useful in studying convergence or long-time existence for given initial data.

1. Introduction This brief article consists of a collection of remarks on the geometry of G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structures on 7 7 -manifolds, some of which are based on old unpublished joint work carried out on separate occasions with two other people: F. Reese Harvey and Steven Altschuler. The work with Reese Harvey (recounted in § 5 ) concerned techniques for calculating various quantities associated to a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure, possibly with torsion, and was carried out intermittently during the period 1988 through 1994. The work with Steven Altschuler (recounted in § 6 ) concerned the geometry of a natural Laplacian flow for G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures and was carried out in 1992. The main reason for making these remarks available now is that some of these formulae and results do not seem to have appeared yet in the literature and some people have expressed an interest in learning about them.

Remark 1 (The vector cross product definition of G 2 {\rm G}_{2} ): Given a vector space V V over ℝ {\mathbb{R}} endowed with a positive definite inner product ⟨ , ⟩ : V × V → ℝ \langle,\rangle:V\times V\to{\mathbb{R}} , a ( 2 2 -fold) vector cross product on ( V , ⟨ , ⟩ ) \bigl(V,\langle,\rangle\bigr) is a skew-symmetric bilinear pairing × : V × V → V \times:V\times V\to V that satisfies (2.34) ⟨ v 1 × v 2 , v 1 ⟩ = 0 and | v 1 × v 2 | 2 = | v 1 | 2 ​ | v 2 | 2 − ⟨ v 1 , v 2 ⟩ 2 \langle v_{1}\times v_{2},v_{1}\rangle=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad|v_{1}\times v_{2}|^{2}=|v_{1}|^{2}\,|v_{2}|^{2}-\langle v_{1},v_{2}\rangle^{2} for all v 1 , v 2 ∈ V v_{1},v_{2}\in V . It can be shown that the GL ⁡ ( 7 , ℝ ) \operatorname{GL}(7,{\mathbb{R}}) -stabilizer of the vector cross product × ϕ \times_{\phi} is equal to G 2 {\rm G}_{2} . Hence one could take × ϕ : ℝ 7 × ℝ 7 → ℝ 7 \times_{\phi}:{\mathbb{R}}^{7}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{7}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{7} as the algebraic structure defining G 2 {\rm G}_{2} . In fact, this is what Gray did in his work on G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures. However, I find that the 3 3 -form formulation is more congenial for computations, so vector cross products will not play any significant role in this article.

Definition 2 (Definite 3 3 -forms on manifolds): A 3 3 -form σ \sigma on M M that takes values in Λ + 3 ​ ( T ∗ ​ M ) \Lambda^{3}_{+}(T^{*}M) will be said to be a definite 3 3 -form on M M . The set of definite 3 3 -forms on M M will be denoted Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \Omega^{3}_{+}(M) .

Remark 2 (Alternative terminologies): Some authors use ‘almost G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure’ to refer to what I am calling a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure in this article. Apparently, this practice stems from an imagined analogy with the distinction between ‘almost complex structure’ and ‘complex structure’. However, for a subgroup G ⊂ GL ⁡ ( n , ℝ ) G\subset\operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{R}}) , the use of ‘ G G -structure’ on an n n -manifold M M to mean a G G -subbundle of the GL ⁡ ( n , ℝ ) \operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{R}}) -bundle of frames (or coframes) on M M is well established. It seems unwise to tamper with this usage, especially since ‘almost G G -structure’ suggests a structure that lacks some property of actual G G -structures. Making an exception for the case G = G 2 G={{\rm G}_{2}} merely invites confusion. This use of ‘ G G -structure’ does not conflict with the ‘almost complex structure’ vs. ‘complex structure’ usage since a complex structure on a 2 ​ n 2n -manifold is not simply a GL ⁡ ( n , ℂ ) \operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{C}}) -structure, but is (by the Newlander-Nirenberg theorem, equivalent to) a GL ⁡ ( n , ℂ ) \operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{C}}) -structure with an assumed integrability property, whereas an ‘almost complex structure’ actually is (equivalent to) a GL ⁡ ( n , ℂ ) \operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{C}}) -structure, not an ‘almost GL ⁡ ( n , ℂ ) \operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{C}}) -structure’. Some authors speak of an ‘integrable G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure’, meaning a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure σ ∈ Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \sigma\in\Omega^{3}_{+}(M) satisfying some differential equations, such as d ​ σ = 0 \mathrm{d}\sigma=0 (the exact differential equation intended varies with the author). Again, this usage appears to stem from an imagined analogy with a symplectic structure, which is defined by a nondegenerate 2 2 -form ω \omega that is closed, i.e., d ​ ω = 0 \mathrm{d}\omega=0 . In the symplectic case, Darboux’ Theorem says that ω \omega is, indeed, locally equivalent to the flat model, i.e., is ‘integrable’ in the standard terminology of the theory of Lie pseudo-groups. (In a similar way, one speaks of ‘integrable almost complex structures’.) This usage of ‘integrable’ for G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures also seems ill-advised to me since, as will be seen below, no first order condition on a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure implies that it is locally equivalent to the flat model (which is the only interpretation of ‘integrable’ in this context that would be consistent with the established usage in the theory of Lie pseudo-groups). Moreover, this encourages the confusing shift of terminology in which ‘ G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure’ is used to mean ‘integrable G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure’ and ‘almost G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure’ is used to mean an actual G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure. For this reason, none of the modifiers ‘integrable’, ‘almost’, ‘nearly’, or their ilk will be used in this article when referring to G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures. However, since it seems to be harmless, the terminology ‘ G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -manifold’ will sometimes be used to denote a manifold endowed with a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure that is flat to first order (i.e., ‘torsion-free’ in the usual terminology).

Definition 3 (Associated metric, orientation, and vector cross product): For any σ ∈ Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \sigma\in\Omega^{3}_{+}(M) , denote by g σ g_{\sigma} , ∗ σ *_{\sigma} , and × σ \times_{\sigma} the metric, Hodge star operator, and vector cross product on M M that are canonically associated to σ \sigma . When it is needed, the oriented orthonormal frame bundle of g σ g_{\sigma} with this orientation will be denoted 𝖥 σ = F σ ⋅ SO ⁡ ( 7 ) \mathsf{F}_{\sigma}=F_{\sigma}\cdot\operatorname{SO}(7) .

Remark 3 (Existence of G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures): Because G 2 {\rm G}_{2} is both connected and simply connected, a connected 7 7 -manifold M M can support a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure only if it is both orientable and spinnable, i.e., if the first two Stiefel-Whitney classes of M M vanish. Conversely, by an observation due to Gray [ 9 ] , these two necessary conditions are also sufficient: Since G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} is simply connected, it is the image under the standard double covering map ρ : Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) → SO ⁡ ( 7 ) \rho:\operatorname{Spin}(7)\to\operatorname{SO}(7) of a unique subgroup of Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{Spin}(7) , which, by abuse of language, will also be called G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} . Now, Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{Spin}(7) has a faithful representation on ℝ 8 {\mathbb{R}}^{8} and hence can be regarded as a subgroup of SO ⁡ ( 8 ) \operatorname{SO}(8) . The restriction of this representation to G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} must also be faithful and hence, for dimension reasons, it must be isomorphic to 𝖵 0 , 0 ⊕ 𝖵 1 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{0,0}\oplus\mathsf{V}_{1,0} . In particular, G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} fixes a vector in ℝ 8 {\mathbb{R}}^{8} and acts transitively on the unit 6 6 -sphere orthogonal to this vector. Consequently, Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{Spin}(7) must act transitively on the unit 7 7 -sphere in ℝ 8 {\mathbb{R}}^{8} with stabilizer subgroup G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} . Now, suppose M 7 M^{7} to be orientable and spinnable. Choose a Riemannian metric g g , an orientation, and a spin structure 𝖥 ~ → M \tilde{\mathsf{F}}\to M , i.e., a spin double cover of the SO ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{SO}(7) -bundle 𝖥 → M \mathsf{F}\to M consisting of oriented, g g -orthonormal coframes on M M . The associated spinor bundle 𝕊 = 𝖥 ~ × Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) ℝ 8 {\mathbb{S}}=\tilde{\mathsf{F}}\times_{\operatorname{Spin}(7)}{\mathbb{R}}^{8} is a vector bundle of rank 8 8 over the 7 7 -manifold M M and therefore has a nonvanishing unit section s : M → 𝕊 s:M\to{\mathbb{S}} . This allows one to reduce the structure group of 𝖥 ~ \tilde{\mathsf{F}} (and hence 𝖥 \mathsf{F} ) from Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{Spin}(7) to G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} (since, by the previous paragraph, this is, up to conjugacy, the Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) \operatorname{Spin}(7) -stablizer of any nonzero vector in ℝ 8 {\mathbb{R}}^{8} ). Thus, M M admits a G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structure whose associated metric and orientation are the chosen ones.

(If H 1 ​ ( M , ℤ 2 ) ≠ 0 H^{1}(M,{\mathbb{Z}}_{2})\not=0 , the pair ( a , α ) (a,\alpha) might only be defined up to sign.) Of course, some such formula was expected, since SO ⁡ ( 7 ) / G 2 ≃ ℝ ​ ℙ 7 \operatorname{SO}(7)/{{\rm G}_{2}}\simeq{\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{7} (a consequence of the result Spin ⁡ ( 7 ) / G 2 ≃ S 7 \operatorname{Spin}(7)/{{\rm G}_{2}}\simeq S^{7} discussed in Remark 3 ). What ( 3.6 ) displays is a concrete isomorphism between the bundle 𝖥 σ / G 2 \mathsf{F}_{\sigma}/{{\rm G}_{2}} and the ℝ ​ ℙ 7 {\mathbb{R}}{\mathbb{P}}^{7} -bundle ℙ ⁡ ( ℝ ⊕ T ∗ ​ M ) {\mathbb{P}}\bigl({\mathbb{R}}\oplus T^{*}M\bigr) over M M .

Proposition 1 (The torsion forms): For any G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure σ ∈ Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \sigma\in\Omega^{3}_{+}(M) , there exist unique differential forms τ 0 ∈ Ω 0 ​ ( M ) \tau_{0}\in\Omega^{0}(M) , τ 1 ∈ Ω 1 ​ ( M ) \tau_{1}\in\Omega^{1}(M) , τ 2 ∈ Ω 14 2 ​ ( M , σ ) \tau_{2}\in\Omega^{2}_{14}(M,\sigma) , and τ 3 ∈ Ω 27 3 ​ ( M , σ ) \tau_{3}\in\Omega^{3}_{27}(M,\sigma) so that the following equations hold: (3.7) d ​ σ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\,\sigma = τ 0 ​ ∗ σ ​ σ + 3 ​ τ 1 ∧ σ + ∗ σ ​ τ 3 , \displaystyle=\tau_{0}\,\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\sigma+3\,\tau_{1}{\mathchoice{\,{\scriptstyle\wedge}\,}{{\scriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}}\sigma+\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\tau_{3}\,, d ​ ∗ σ ​ σ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\,\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\sigma = 4 ​ τ 1 ∧ ∗ σ ​ σ + τ 2 ∧ σ . \displaystyle=\qquad 4\,\tau_{1}{\mathchoice{\,{\scriptstyle\wedge}\,}{{\scriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}}\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\sigma+\tau_{2}{\mathchoice{\,{\scriptstyle\wedge}\,}{{\scriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\wedge}}}\sigma\,.

Definition 4 (The torsion forms): For a definite 3 3 -form σ ∈ Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \sigma\in\Omega^{3}_{+}(M) , the quadruple of forms ( τ 0 , τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 ) (\tau_{0},\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3}) defined by ( 3.7 ) will be referred to as the intrinsic torsion forms of σ \sigma .

Remark 5 (General intrinsic torsion): The existence of the identity ( 3.8 ) may seem surprising at first, but the existence of such an identity can be understood by general considerations. For any subgroup G ⊂ SO ⁡ ( n ) G\subset\operatorname{SO}(n) , the first order invariants (usually called the ‘intrinsic torsion’) of a G G -structure F F on an n n -manifold M M take values in a bundle over M M associated to the natural G G -representation on ( 𝔰 ​ 𝔬 ( n ) / 𝔤 ) ⊗ ℝ n (\operatorname{\mathfrak{so}}(n)/\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}})\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{n} . (See § 4.2 below for a further explication of this fact.) When the first order invariants of a given G G -structure vanish, it is said to be ‘ 1 1 -flat’ or ‘flat to first order’. For more discussion of this notion, see [ 2 ] .

Proposition 2 ( 1 1 -flatness of G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures): A G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure σ ∈ Ω + 3 ​ ( M ) \sigma\in\Omega^{3}_{+}(M) is flat to first order if and only if its torsion forms all vanish, i.e., if and only if d ​ σ = d ​ ∗ σ ​ σ = 0 \mathrm{d}\sigma=\mathrm{d}\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\sigma=0 .

Remark 6 (Fernández and Gray’s theorem on vector cross products): Proposition 2 implies the 1982 result of Fernández and Gray [ 6 ] that a vector cross product × : T ​ M × T ​ M → T ​ M \times:TM{\times}TM\to TM that is compatible with a Riemannian metric g g on M M is g g -parallel if and only if the corresponding 3 3 -form is closed and coclosed (with respect to g g ). The essential difference between Proposition 2 and their result is that they assume a specific metric g g and vector cross product to be given, whereas Proposition 2 starts with a definite 3 3 -form σ \sigma and constructs a specific metric associated to σ \sigma .

Remark 7 (Canonical connections): The use of the term ‘natural’ with regard to the connection ` on the G G -structure F F should not be construed to mean that this is the only ‘canonical’ connection on M M that is compatible with F F . In many cases, this is only one of a family of possible ‘canonical’ connections that can be defined in terms of the first-order invariants of the G G -structure F F and that are preserved under equivalence of G G -structures. For example, if the G G -modules V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 ) V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}) and 𝔤 ⊗ ℝ n \operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{n} have common constituents, so that the space Hom G ⁡ ( V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 ) , 𝔤 ⊗ ℝ n ) \Hom^{G}\bigl(V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}),\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\bigr) of G G -equivariant homomorphisms between the two spaces has dimension r > 0 r>0 , there will be an r r -parameter family of ways of modifying ` , by adding a 𝔤 \operatorname{\mathfrak{g}} -valued 1 1 -form whose coefficients are linear in the torsion functions, in such a way that the resulting modification defines a connection on M M compatible with the G G -structure F F . Each element in this r r -parameter family of connections can be regarded as canonical in the sense that equivalence of G G -structures will induce isomorphisms between the corresponding connections in the r r -parameter family. Of course, there is no a priori reason to consider only connection modifications that are linear in the torsion functions; for example, any G G -equivariant polynomial mapping V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 ) → 𝔤 ⊗ ℝ n V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}})\to\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{n} could be used to define such a modification of ` . However, these ‘higher’ modifications do not often arise in practice. Depending on the intended use, it could well be that one of these other connections (rather than the one being called ‘natural’ in the present article) is better suited for expressing identities of one kind or another.

Remark 8 (Canonical G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -connections): Since 𝔤 2 ⊗ 𝖵 1 , 0 = 𝖵 1 , 0 ⊕ 𝖵 2 , 0 ⊕ 𝖵 1 , 1 \operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}\otimes\mathsf{V}_{1,0}=\mathsf{V}_{1,0}\oplus\mathsf{V}_{2,0}\oplus\mathsf{V}_{1,1} shares two G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -irreducible modules with V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 ) V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}) , it follows from Remark 7 that there is actually a 2 2 -parameter family of canonical connections associated to any G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structure σ \sigma . Each element in this family is compatible with σ \sigma (in the sense that σ \sigma is parallel under the corresponding parallel translation). Since the common constituents 𝖵 1 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{1,0} and 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} correspond to the torsion forms τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 3 \tau_{3} , respectively, it follows that the entire two-parameter family of canonical connections collapses to a single connection if and only if the G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structure σ \sigma satisfies τ 1 = τ 3 = 0 \tau_{1}=\tau_{3}=0 . In this case, differentiating the equations ( 3.7 ) shows that τ 0 ​ τ 2 = 0 \tau_{0}\tau_{2}=0 and d ​ τ 0 = 0 \mathrm{d}\tau_{0}=0 . In particular, when M M is connected, it follows that τ 0 \tau_{0} is constant. If τ 0 = 0 \tau_{0}=0 , then the G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structure is closed. If τ 0 ≠ 0 \tau_{0}\not=0 , then τ 2 = 0 \tau_{2}=0 and one has the equation d ​ σ = τ 0 ​ ∗ σ ​ σ \mathrm{d}\sigma=\tau_{0}\,\mskip 1.0mu\mathord{*\kern-0.5pt_{\sigma}}\mskip 1.0mu\sigma , which is the defining equation for the so-called ‘nearly G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -manifolds’. Thus, the family of canonical G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -connections associated to a G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -structure σ \sigma collapses to a single G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -connection if and only if either σ \sigma is closed or it defines a nearly G 2 {{\rm G}_{2}} -manifold.

Remark 9 (Covariant differentials): The decisive advantage of using the forms D ​ ø D\hbox{\teneur\char 28\relax} and D ​ ` D\hbox{\teneur\char 18\relax} to express the curvature tensor is that these forms do not contain all of the information about the second order invariants of the underlying G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure σ \sigma although they do contain enough information to recover the Riemann curvature tensor of the underlying metric.

Remark 10 (General identities): It is perhaps worth remarking on why the identities ( 4.28 ) and ( 4.30 ) could be expected to have the form that they do. In the first place, one knows that the scalar curvature must be expressible in a G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -invariant manner as a sum of a linear expression in the second order invariants, i.e., a section of a vector bundle modeled on V 2 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) , and an expression in the first order invariants, i.e., the torsion forms, that is at most quadratic. A glance at ( 4.7 ) shows that there is only one trivial summand in the representation V 2 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) and hence there is essentially only one possible second order term up to a universal constant multiple. Since δ ​ τ 1 \delta\tau_{1} is a scalar second order invariant, it must represent this copy of 𝖵 0 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{0,0} in V 2 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) . As for the first order terms, since V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) consists of four mutually inequivalent G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -modules, the space of G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -invariant quadratic forms on this space has dimension 4 4 and must be represented by the square norms of the four torsion forms. Thus, a formula of the form ( 4.28 ) was inevitable; it was just a matter of determining the numerical coefficients, which was done with the aid of Maple . The argument for the form of ( 4.30 ) is quite similar. Since the scalar curvature has already been determined, it is a question of writing down a formula for the trace-free part of the Ricci tensor, i.e., finding linear terms in V 2 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) and quadratic terms in V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) that take values in the G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -module 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} . Again, a glance at ( 4.7 ) shows that there are at most three possible second order terms and it is not difficult to see that the three second order terms that take values in 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} found by taking derivatives of τ 1 \tau_{1} , τ 2 \tau_{2} , and τ 3 \tau_{3} and projecting into a suitable 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} representation are, in fact, independent and generate the three copies of 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} that appear in V 2 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) . On the other hand, using representation theory to compute the second symmetric power of V 1 ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) shows that there exist eight copies of 𝖵 2 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{2,0} in this symmetric power. Of those eight copies, five are computable via wedge product and appear in the formula for Ricci. Of the remaining three, one bilinear in τ 2 \tau_{2} and τ 3 \tau_{3} and the other two quadratic in τ 3 \tau_{3} , only one of the terms quadratic in τ 3 \tau_{3} actually makes an appearance. The rest is just a matter of determining constants.

Remark 11 (Differential invariants of closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures): Just as one can compute the dimension of the space of k k -jets of G G -structures as in § 4.2 , one can compute the dimension of the space of k k -jets of G G -structures satisfying some set of differential equations. In the case of closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structures, denote the module of k k -th order differential invariants by V k ′ ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) ⊂ V k ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V^{\prime}_{k}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2})\subset V_{k}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) . One finds, for example, that (4.38) V 1 ′ ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) ≃ 𝖵 0 , 1 V 2 ′ ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) ≃ 𝖵 2 , 0 ⊕ 𝖵 1 , 1 ⊕ 𝖵 0 , 2 . V^{\prime}_{1}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2})\simeq\mathsf{V}_{0,1}\qquad\qquad V^{\prime}_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2})\simeq\mathsf{V}_{2,0}\oplus\mathsf{V}_{1,1}\oplus\mathsf{V}_{0,2}. This implies, on abstract grounds, that the scalar curvature of the underlying metric of a closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure must be expressed in terms of the first order invariants (since there is no 𝖵 0 , 0 \mathsf{V}_{0,0} component in V 2 ′ ​ ( 𝔤 2 ) V^{\prime}_{2}(\operatorname{\mathfrak{g}}_{2}) ) and that the full Ricci tensor can be expressed in terms of τ 2 \tau_{2} and d ​ τ 2 \mathrm{d}\tau_{2} . Thus, the form of ( 4.36 ) and ( 4.37 ) could have been anticipated, if not the numerical coefficients. Of course, it is easy to ‘write down’ the general closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure locally: If β ∈ Ω 2 ​ ( ℝ 7 ) \beta\in\Omega^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{7}) is a (smooth) 2 2 -form that vanishes to second order at 0 ∈ ℝ 7 0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{7} , then the 3 3 -form σ = ϕ + d ​ β \sigma=\phi+\mathrm{d}\beta will equal ϕ \phi at 0 0 and hence will be a closed, definite 3 3 -form on some open neighborhood of 0 ∈ ℝ 7 0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{7} . Conversely, if σ \sigma is a closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure on a manifold M 7 M^{7} , then any point p ∈ M p\in M has an open neighborhood U U on which there exists a p p -centered coordinate chart x : U → ℝ 7 x:U\to{\mathbb{R}}^{7} such that σ U = x ∗ ​ ( ϕ + d ​ β ) \sigma_{U}=x^{*}(\phi+\mathrm{d}\beta) where β ∈ Ω 2 ​ ( ℝ 7 ) \beta\in\Omega^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{7}) is a 2 2 -form that vanishes to second order at 0 ∈ ℝ 7 0\in{\mathbb{R}}^{7} . In a sense that it is possible to make precise using Cartan’s notion of the generality of the space of solutions of a system of pde , one can develop this discussion further to show that the general closed G 2 {\rm G}_{2} -structure modulo diffeomorphism depends on 8 8 functions of seven variables.
